opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, they're very different kinds of hard. During my PhD, the challenge was mostly intellectual and very focused. I could spend weeks thinking about one problem — how to make a compiler generate efficient sparse data structure code, or how to make a differentiable physics simulator actually work. The feedback loop was fairly clear: you have an idea, you implement it, you run experiments, you write the paper. And most of the time, the person you were really accountable to was yourself and your advisor.

Being a CEO is much more about context switching. In a single day I might go from a technical design discussion, to a hiring conversation, to talking with investors, to thinking about what customers actually need. You don't get to go deep on one thing for very long, and that was a real adjustment for me, because by nature I'm someone who likes to sit down and write code for hours.

The other big difference is responsibility. In a PhD, if an experiment fails, it's your own time you lost. As a CEO, there are people who left good jobs to join you, and their careers and livelihoods are partly tied to the decisions you make. That's a kind of weight I didn't really feel before.

That said, I think the PhD trained me well in some ways. Research teaches you to deal with uncertainty — most of your ideas don't work, and you have to keep going anyway. Startups are very similar. You're constantly making decisions with incomplete information, and you need that same persistence. So I'd say the PhD was hard in depth, and being a CEO is hard in breadth. Both are tiring, but in different ways, and I've learned a lot from each.

r001.rationale: The response says CEO responsibility for employees’ careers and livelihoods carries weight, but it does not attribute greater exhaustion as CEO than during the PhD to that responsibility; it says both are tiring in different ways.

r002.rationale: The response describes CEO context switching, but does not say company growth forces Hu to handle matters outside his strengths.

r003.rationale: The response does not say entrepreneurship helped Hu correct flaws in his personality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the two feel like completely different sports.

During my PhD at MIT, the hardest part was depth. I'd spend months on a single problem, like getting Taichi's compiler to do the right thing, or figuring out why a simulation was unstable. The feedback loop was slow, but the problem was well defined. I could close the door, think for a week, and eventually there was a right answer. Success was something I could mostly control with my own effort.

Being a CEO is the opposite. It's breadth, and the feedback loop is both faster and noisier. On a given day I might go from a technical discussion about GPU kernels, to a hiring decision, to a customer who's unhappy, to thinking about how much runway we have. None of those have a clean "correct" solution, and most of them don't depend only on me. The biggest shift was realizing that my job isn't to solve the problem myself anymore, it's to build a team and an environment where the problem gets solved. For someone who got where they are by being good at personally writing code, that's a real identity adjustment.

The emotional side is also different. In a PhD, when an experiment fails, it's your experiment. As a CEO, when something goes wrong, it affects people's jobs and livelihoods, and that weight sits with you constantly. I sleep less well than I did as a student, which says something, because PhD students don't sleep great either.

What's the same is that both reward stubbornness and curiosity. The research habit of asking "why does this actually work" turns out to be incredibly useful when you're running a company, because so much of business advice is folklore. I just try to apply the same skepticism to our strategy that I used to apply to a benchmark result.

r001.rationale: He says CEO problems affect people's jobs and livelihoods and that this weight sits with him constantly, contrasting it with a failed PhD experiment being his own.

r002.rationale: He describes the CEO role as broad and spanning technical, hiring, customer, and financial matters, but does not say company growth forces him to learn to handle matters outside his strengths.

r003.rationale: He mentions curiosity, stubbornness, and skepticism as useful in both roles, but does not say entrepreneurship helped correct flaws in his personality.

astra-6.text:
For me, the biggest difference is how I spend my attention. During a PhD, you can focus deeply on one problem for a long time. As a CEO, you have to switch between different problems—technology, people, customers—and decide which ones actually need your attention.

There’s also a different kind of responsibility. In research, you’re mostly thinking about whether you can make an idea work. As a CEO, you have to think about whether the team can make it work together. So working harder yourself isn’t always the answer. Sometimes the most useful thing you can do is give people clarity and let them move forward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that, during a PhD, you can focus very deeply on one problem. You have a lot of control over how you spend your time, and your progress depends largely on your own work. As a CEO, your attention has to move between many different problems, and you have to help other people make progress, too.

That requires a different mindset. You can’t personally solve everything, even if you want to. You have to decide what matters most, communicate that clearly, and trust the team. For me, the challenge is balancing that responsibility with the desire to spend uninterrupted time on technical work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts CEO responsibilities with PhD work, but does not say being responsible for others makes him more exhausted.

r003.rationale: It discusses a different mindset and trusting the team, but does not say entrepreneurship has helped correct personality flaws.
